claim: Nosocomial acquisition of SARS-CoV-2 in geriatric institutions and long-term care facilities may account for large proportions of all declared COVID-19 cases in many countries.
source: Nosocomial acquisition of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) in geriatric institutions and long-term care facilities (LTCFs) may account for large proportions of all declared coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) cases in many countries, and contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality (Thiabaud et al., 2021; Bhattacharya et al., 2021; The Guardian, 2021b; The Guardian, 2021a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Nosocomial acquisition of SARS-CoV-2 in geriatric institutions and long-term care facilities contributes substantially to morbidity and mortality.
source: Nosocomial acquisition of severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) in geriatric institutions and long-term care facilities (LTCFs) may account for large proportions of all declared coronavirus disease 2019 (Covid-19) cases in many countries, and contribute substantially to morbidity and mortality (Thiabaud et al., 2021; Bhattacharya et al., 2021; The Guardian, 2021b; The Guardian, 2021a).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The reservoir of SARS-CoV-2 in healthcare environments may contribute to amplifying the pandemic.
source: Because the reservoir of SARS-CoV-2 in healthcare environments may contribute to amplifying the pandemic (Knight et al., 2022), we need to better understand transmission dynamics in these settings.
evidence: Supported by citation to Knight et al., 2022

claim: Healthcare workers can be victims and/or vectors of SARS-CoV-2 infection.
source: The role of healthcare workers (HCWs) in nosocomial Covid-19 transmission dynamics is complex, as they can be victims and/or vectors of SARS-CoV-2 infection, and can acquire from or transmit to their peers and patients and the community (Abbas et al., 2021b; Ellingford et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbas et al., 2021b and Ellingford et al., 2021

claim: Healthcare workers can acquire SARS-CoV-2 from or transmit to their peers, patients, and the community.
source: The role of healthcare workers (HCWs) in nosocomial Covid-19 transmission dynamics is complex, as they can be victims and/or vectors of SARS-CoV-2 infection, and can acquire from or transmit to their peers and patients and the community (Abbas et al., 2021b; Ellingford et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Abbas et al., 2021b and Ellingford et al., 2021

claim: There is ongoing controversy and uncertainty surrounding the role of HCWs in infecting patients during nosocomial outbreaks.
source: There is ongoing controversy and uncertainty surrounding the role of HCWs in infecting patients during nosocomial outbreaks, and findings from acute-care hospitals cannot be applied directly to LTCFs and geriatric hospitals (Abbas et al., 2021a; Klompas et al., 2021; Lucey et al., 2021; Aggarwal et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: Findings from acute-care hospitals cannot be applied directly to LTCFs and geriatric hospitals.
source: There is ongoing controversy and uncertainty surrounding the role of HCWs in infecting patients during nosocomial outbreaks, and findings from acute-care hospitals cannot be applied directly to LTCFs and geriatric hospitals (Abbas et al., 2021a; Klompas et al., 2021; Lucey et al., 2021; Aggarwal et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to published literature

claim: The Hospital of Geriatrics has 196 acute-care and 100 rehabilitation beds.
source: The Hospital of Geriatrics, part of the Geneva University Hospitals (HUG) consortium, has 196 acute-care and 100 rehabilitation beds.
evidence: Direct statement about the hospital setting

claim: During the first pandemic wave, a maximum of 176 acute-care beds were dedicated to admitting geriatric patients with COVID-19 who were not eligible for escalation of therapy.
source: During the first pandemic wave, a maximum of 176 acute-care beds were dedicated to admitting geriatric patients with Covid-19 who were not eligible for escalation of therapy (e.g., intensive care unit admission) (Mendes et al., 2020).
evidence: Direct statement about hospital operations with citation

claim: Beginning on 1 April 2020, RT-PCR was used to screen all patients on admission for SARS-CoV-2.
source: Beginning on 1 April 2020, we use RT-PCR to screen all patients on admission for SARS-CoV-2.
evidence: Direct statement about screening protocol

claim: Between 7 April 2020 and 30 May 2020, patients in non-Covid wards were screened.
source: Between 7 April 2020 and 30 May 2020, we screened patients in non-Covid wards.
evidence: Direct statement about screening protocol

claim: HCWs from outbreak wards were encouraged to undergo PCR testing on nasopharyngeal swabs between 9 and 16 April 2020, even if they were asymptomatic.
source: We encouraged HCWs from outbreak wards to undergo PCR testing on nasopharyngeal swabs between 9 and 16 April 2020, even if they were asymptomatic.
evidence: Direct statement about testing protocol

claim: Healthcare-associated COVID-19 was defined by an onset of symptoms ≥5 days after admission in conjunction with a strong suspicion of healthcare transmission.
source: We defined healthcare-associated (HA) Covid-19 by an onset of symptoms ≥5 days after admission in conjunction with a strong suspicion of healthcare transmission, in accordance with Swissnoso guidelines (Swissnoso, 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of definition with citation to guidelines

claim: An outbreak was declared when ≥3 cases of HA-COVID-19 (HCWs and patients) with a possible temporal-spatial link were identified.
source: An outbreak was declared when ≥3 cases of HA-Covid-19 (HCWs and patients) with a possible temporal-spatial link were identified (Swissnoso, 2021).
evidence: Direct statement of definition with citation to guidelines

claim: During the study period (1 March to 7 May 2020), 180 SARS-CoV-2 positive cases were included: 127 HCWs (91 HCWcovid, 36 HCWoutbreak) and 53 patients.
source: During the study period (1 March to 7 May 2020), we included 180 SARS-CoV-2 positive cases: 127 HCWs (91 HCWcovid, 36 HCWoutbreak) and 53 patients.
evidence: Direct statement of study results

claim: Of the 53 included patients, 4 likely acquired COVID-19 in the community.
source: Of the 53 included patients, post hoc epidemiological analysis showed that 4 of these likely acquired Covid-19 in the community (CA-Covid-19).
evidence: Direct statement of analysis results

claim: The 49 nosocomial cases represented 20.2% (49/242) of all patients hospitalised with COVID-19.
source: The remaining 49 nosocomial cases represented 20.2% (49/242) of all patients hospitalised with Covid-19, and 81.7% (49/60) of nosocomial Covid-19 cases in the Geriatric Hospital.
evidence: Direct statement with calculated proportion

claim: The 49 nosocomial cases represented 81.7% (49/60) of nosocomial COVID-19 cases in the Geriatric Hospital.
source: The remaining 49 nosocomial cases represented 20.2% (49/242) of all patients hospitalised with Covid-19, and 81.7% (49/60) of nosocomial Covid-19 cases in the Geriatric Hospital.
evidence: Direct statement with calculated proportion

claim: The ward-level attack rates ranged from 10% to 19% among patients.
source: The ward-level attack rates ranged from 10% to 19% among patients.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated attack rates

claim: 21% of all HCWs in the geriatric hospital had a PCR-positive test.
source: Moreover, 21% of all HCWs in the geriatric hospital had a PCR-positive test.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated proportion

claim: The time period between date of onset of symptoms and date of swab was shorter for HCWcovid (mean 1.6 days, SD 1.78) than for HCWoutbreak (mean 2.88 days, SD 4.84).
source: Strikingly, the time period between date of onset of symptoms and date of swab was shorter for HCWcovid (mean 1.6 days, SD 1.78) than for HCWoutbreak (mean 2.88 days, SD 4.84).
evidence: Direct statement of calculated statistics

claim: SARS-CoV-2 sequences were obtained for 148 isolates of the 180 cases (82.2%), including 105 HCWs (82.7%) and 43 patients (81.1%).
source: We obtained SARS-CoV-2 sequences for 148 isolates of the 180 cases (82.2%), including 105 HCWs (82.7%) and 43 patients (81.1%).
evidence: Direct statement of sequencing results

claim: A rooted phylogenetic tree found substantial genetic diversity, with at least nine clusters and sub-clusters.
source: A rooted phylogenetic tree found substantial genetic diversity, with at least nine clusters and sub-clusters (Figure 2).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2

claim: 22 imports in total (17 HCWs, 5 patients) with posterior support ≥10% were identified from the reconstructed trees.
source: From the reconstructed trees, we identified 22 imports in total (17 HCWs, 5 patients) with posterior support ≥10%.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: The 22 imported cases generated 41 secondary cases (posterior support ≥10%), with a median posterior support of 32.4% (IQR 17.0%–53.7%).
source: The 22 imported cases generated 41 secondary cases (posterior support ≥10%), with a median posterior support of 32.4% (IQR 17.0%–53.7%).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: When restricting to imports with ≥50% posterior support, there were 16 imported cases (12 HCWs, 4 patients), generating 35 secondary cases.
source: When restricting to imports with ≥50% posterior support, there were 16 imported cases 16 (12 HCWs, 4 patients), generating 35 secondary cases.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: The model estimated that the reporting probability was 91.2% (95% credible interval [CrI] 86.6%–95.2%), suggesting that only 8.8% of source cases involved in transmission were not identified.
source: The model estimated that the reporting probability was 91.2% (95% credible interval [CrI] 86.6%–95.2%), suggesting that only 8.8% of source cases involved in transmission were not identified.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with inference

claim: For most (90.8%) cases, the model identified the direct infector, without intermediate unobserved cases.
source: For most (90.8%) cases, the model identified the direct infector, without intermediate unobserved cases (Figure 3—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with reference to figure

claim: The epidemiological attribution of the presumptive ward on which patients became infected and that suggested by the model output agree for 95% of the nosocomial cases.
source: The epidemiological attribution of the presumptive ward on which patients became infected and that suggested by the model output (see Appendix 1) agree for 95% of the nosocomial cases.
evidence: Direct statement comparing epidemiological and model results

claim: Among patient-to-patient transmission events, 95.2% (95% CrI 84.2%–100%) involved patients who shared a ward during their hospital stay.
source: Among patient-to-patient transmission events, and across all posterior trees, 95.2% (95% CrI 84.2%–100%) involved patients who shared a ward during their hospital stay.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: Only 19.7% (95% CrI 6.7%–33.3%) of patient-to-patient transmissions involved patients who had shared a room.
source: In contrast, only 19.7% (95% CrI 6.7%–33.3%) of patient-to-patient transmissions involved patients who had shared a room.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: The number of secondary infections caused by each infected case ranged from 0 to 9.
source: The number of secondary infections caused by each infected case (individual reproductive number R, estimated from the transmission tree reconstruction), ranged from 0 to 9 (Figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 4

claim: The proportion of non-transmitters among both HCWoutbreak and patientnoso was smaller in the early than in the late stage (approximately 32% in early and 55% in late phase for both groups).
source: We found that the proportion of non-transmitters among both HCWoutbreak and patientnoso was smaller in the early than in the late stage (approximately 32% in early and 55% in late phase for both groups), suggesting that the contribution of these groups to ongoing transmission decreased over the study period.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with inference

claim: The contribution of HCWoutbreak and patientnoso to ongoing transmission decreased over the study period.
source: We found that the proportion of non-transmitters among both HCWoutbreak and patientnoso was smaller in the early than in the late stage (approximately 32% in early and 55% in late phase for both groups), suggesting that the contribution of these groups to ongoing transmission decreased over the study period.
evidence: Inference drawn from the data on non-transmitters

claim: The proportion of non-transmitters among HCWcovid was stable at about 55%–60% across the early and the late phase.
source: Conversely, the proportion of non-transmitters among HCWcovid was stable at about 55%–60% across the early and the late phase.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: The proportions of high transmitters were higher among HCWoutbreak than either patientnoso or HCWcovid in the late phases (28.6% vs. 11.8% and 13.9%) of the outbreak.
source: The proportions of high transmitters were higher among HCWoutbreak than either patientnoso or HCWcovid in the late phases (28.6% vs. 11.8% and 13.9%) of the outbreak.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: Due to small numbers, the differences in proportions of high transmitters were not statistically significant.
source: However, due to small numbers, these differences were not statistically significant.
evidence: Direct statement about statistical significance

claim: Cases were significantly less likely than expected at random to be infected by HCWs from COVID wards (proportion infected by HCWcovid, fHCW=42%; 95% CrI 36%–49% vs. 53% expected at random; 95% CrI 44%–62%; p=0.042).
source: We found that cases were significantly less likely than expected at random to be infected by HCWs from COVID wards (proportion infected by HCWcovid, fHCW=42%; 95% CrI 36%–49% vs. 53% expected at random; 95% CrI 44%–62%; p=0.042).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with statistical test

claim: HCWoutbreak were significantly more likely than expected at random to become infected by other HCWoutbreak (proportion infected by HCWoutbreak, foutbreak = 38%, 95% CrI 22%–52% v. 18%; 95% CrI 4%–35%, p=0.03).
source: Conversely HCWoutbreak were significantly more likely than expected at random to become infected by other HCWoutbreak (proportion infected by HCWoutbreak, foutbreak = 38%, 95% CrI 22%–52% v. 18%; 95% CrI 4%–35%, p=0.03).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with statistical test

claim: Patients with nosocomial Covid-19 (patientnoso) were significantly more likely than expected at random to be infected by other patientnoso (proportion infected by patientnoso, fpat=56%, 95% CrI 41%–71% vs. 28%; 95% CrI 14%–45%, p=0.005).
source: Patients with nosocomial Covid-19 (patientnoso) were significantly more likely than expected at random to be infected by other patientnoso (proportion infected by patientnoso, fpat=56%, 95% CrI 41%–71% vs. 28%; 95% CrI 14%–45%, p=0.005).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with statistical test

claim: Infected staff or patients in outbreak wards were responsible for significantly more transmission in general (54%; 95% CrI 48%–61%) than expected (43.7%, 95% CrI 35%–53%).
source: Infected staff or patients in outbreak wards were responsible for significantly more transmission in general (54%; 95% CrI 48%–61%) than expected (43.7%, 95% CrI 35%–53%).
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results

claim: Within-ward transmission was more pronounced in outbreak wards (mean 48%; range: 20%–70% of all infections within a ward) than in non-outbreak wards (mean 14%; range 0%–63%).
source: Within-ward transmission was more pronounced in outbreak wards (mean 48%; range: 20%–70% of all infections within a ward) than in non-outbreak wards (mean 14%; range 0%–63%) as shown in Appendix 1—figures 2 and 3.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling results with reference to figures

claim: The combination of epidemiological and genetic data using sophisticated modelling enabled teasing out overall transmission patterns.
source: First, we showed that the combination of epidemiological and genetic data using sophisticated modelling enabled us to tease out overall transmission patterns.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: Transmission dynamics among HCWs differed according to whether they worked in Covid wards or in wards where outbreaks occurred.
source: Second, we showed that transmission dynamics among HCWs differed according to whether they worked in Covid wards or in wards where outbreaks occurred.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: HCW-to-HCW transmission in Covid wards was not higher than expected.
source: We found that HCW-to-HCW transmission in Covid wards was not higher than expected but the risk of transmission between HCWs in non-Covid wards was twofold higher than expected.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: The risk of transmission between HCWs in non-Covid wards was twofold higher than expected.
source: We found that HCW-to-HCW transmission in Covid wards was not higher than expected but the risk of transmission between HCWs in non-Covid wards was twofold higher than expected.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: Excess patient-to-patient transmission events were identified, most of which occurred within the same ward, but not necessarily the same room.
source: Third, we identified excess patient-to-patient transmission events, most of which occurred within the same ward, but not necessarily the same room.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: Multiple importation events were identified that led to a substantial number of secondary cases or clusters; most were related to HCWs, but one was related to a patient with community-acquired Covid-19.
source: Fourth, we identified multiple importation events that led to a substantial number of secondary cases or clusters; most were related to HCWs, but one was related to a patient with community-acquired Covid-19.
evidence: Direct statement summarizing study findings

claim: Settings which care for elderly patients, such as geriatrics and rehabilitation clinics or LTCFs have high attack rates of SARS-CoV-2 for both patients and HCWs.
source: These results are particularly important, as settings which care for elderly patients, such as geriatrics and rehabilitation clinics or LTCFs have high attack rates of SARS-CoV-2 for both patients and HCWs (Abbas et al., 2021b).
evidence: Supported by citation to Abbas et al., 2021b

claim: In an institution-wide seroprevalence study in the hospital consortium, the Department of Rehabilitation and Geriatrics had the highest proportion of HCWs with anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies.
source: In an institution-wide seroprevalence study in our hospital consortium, the Department of Rehabilitation and Geriatrics, of which the hospital in this study was part, had the highest proportion of HCWs with anti-SARS-CoV-2 antibodies (Martischang et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citation to Martischang et al., 2022

claim: HCWs caring for Covid-19 patients were concerned about becoming infected while caring for patients, and therefore may apply IPC measures more rigorously than when caring for patients who do not have Covid-19.
source: Indeed, a previous study Ottolenghi et al., 2021 found that HCWs caring for Covid-19 patients were concerned about becoming infected while caring for patients, and therefore may apply IPC measures more rigorously than when caring for patients who do not have Covid-19.
evidence: Supported by citation to Ottolenghi et al., 2021

claim: HCWs working in non-Covid wards may not have felt threatened by Covid-19 patients who were in principle allocated to other wards, and thus not in their direct care.
source: HCWs working in non-Covid wards may not have felt threatened by Covid-19 patients who were in principle allocated to other wards, and thus not in their direct care.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed transmission patterns

claim: HCWs in non-Covid wards may have underestimated the transmission risk from their peers to a greater extent than those working in Covid wards, and thus may not have maintained physical distancing well.
source: HCWs in non-Covid wards also may have underestimated the transmission risk from their peers to a greater extent than those working in Covid wards, and thus may not have maintained physical distancing well.
evidence: Speculative explanation for observed transmission patterns

claim: A higher mean duration (2.9 days) of presenteeism despite symptoms compatible with Covid-19 was found among HCWs working in non-Covid wards than for those working in Covid wards (1.6 days).
source: In addition, we found a higher mean duration (2.9 days) of presenteeism despite symptoms compatible with Covid-19 among HCWs working in non-Covid wards than for those working in Covid wards (1.6 days), which gives credence to the abovementioned possible explanations for the different transmission patterns.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated statistics with inference

claim: Mathematical models have suggested that single-room isolation of suspected cases could potentially reduce the incidence of nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission by up to 35%.
source: Mathematical models have suggested that single-room isolation of suspected cases could potentially reduce the incidence of nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission by up to 35% (Evans et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Evans et al., 2021

claim: Symptomatic patients were identified promptly, with a median delay of 0 days between symptom onset and their first positive test.
source: In the outbreaks we describe, symptomatic patients were identified promptly, with a median delay of 0 days between symptom onset and their first positive test.
evidence: Direct statement of calculated statistics

claim: Patients may transmit the virus when they are pre-symptomatic.
source: However, these precautions may not be sufficient as patients may transmit the virus when they are pre-symptomatic (Ferretti et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ferretti et al., 2020

claim: Exposure to community-acquired cases who were identified and segregated or cohorted was associated with half the risk of infection compared with exposure to hospital-acquired cases or HCWs who may be asymptomatic.
source: For example, a previous study Mo et al., 2021 found that exposure to community-acquired cases who were identified and segregated or cohorted was associated with half the risk of infection compared with exposure to hospital-acquired cases or HCWs who may be asymptomatic.
evidence: Supported by citation to Mo et al., 2021

claim: Patients with CA-Covid may have passed the peak of infectiousness when they are admitted, whereas patients with HA-Covid cases have frequent unprotected contact with HCWs and other patients during their period of peak infectiousness.
source: One possible explanation for this finding is that patients with CA-Covid may have passed the peak of infectiousness when they are admitted, whereas patients with HA-Covid cases have frequent unprotected contact with HCWs and other patients during their period of peak infectiousness.
evidence: Speculative explanation for findings from cited study

claim: The current evidence does not support the use of real-time genomics for control of SARS-CoV-2 nosocomial outbreaks.
source: The current evidence does not support the use of real-time genomics for control of SARS-CoV-2 nosocomial outbreaks (Stirrup et al., 2021; Stirrup et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Stirrup et al., 2021 and 2022

claim: The outbreaks were controlled without using WGS.
source: Although we were able to gain considerable insight from the powerful combination of genetic sequencing data and rich epidemiological data, we controlled the outbreaks without using WGS, as was the case in many published reports (Arons et al., 2020; Taylor et al., 2020).
evidence: Direct statement with citations to similar studies

claim: WGS may be more useful for ruling out transmission rather than for confirmatory purposes, due to the low number of mutations accumulated in the SARS-CoV-2 genome between transmission pairs.
source: Furthermore, WGS may be more useful for ruling out transmission rather than for confirmatory purposes, due to the low number of mutations accumulated in the SARS-CoV-2 genome between transmission pairs (Braun et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Braun et al., 2021

claim: WGS was performed on isolates from a high proportion (80%) of cases, including those from HCWs which has been previously shown to improve understanding of transmission dynamics.
source: We performed WGS on isolates from a high proportion (80%) of cases, including those from HCWs which has been previously shown to improve understanding of transmission dynamics (Ellingford et al., 2021).
evidence: Direct statement with citation to Ellingford et al., 2021

claim: The data were collected prospectively, thereby minimising the risk of bias.
source: In addition, we collected the data prospectively, thereby minimising the risk of bias.
evidence: Direct statement about study design

claim: The method used to reconstruct who infected whom is able to cope with and identify missing intermediate cases.
source: However the method we used to reconstruct who infected whom is able to cope with and identify missing intermediate cases, which allowed us to estimate that the overwhelming majority of cases (91.5%) was captured in our sample.
evidence: Direct statement about modeling method with inference

claim: The overwhelming majority of cases (91.5%) was captured in the sample.
source: However the method we used to reconstruct who infected whom is able to cope with and identify missing intermediate cases, which allowed us to estimate that the overwhelming majority of cases (91.5%) was captured in our sample.

claim: The investigations were performed during the first pandemic wave with a wild-type variant of SARS-CoV-2 in a susceptible population.
source: In addition, we performed these investigations during the first pandemic wave with a wild-type variant of SARS-CoV-2 in a susceptible population.
evidence: Direct statement about study context

claim: The results may no longer be applicable in settings with high vaccination coverage and/or substantial natural immunity, or in later stages of the pandemic.
source: For these reasons, the results may no longer be applicable in settings with high vaccination coverage and/or substantial natural immunity, or in later stages of the pandemic, also due to accrued experience in managing and preventing outbreaks.
evidence: Inference about generalizability of results

claim: The lessons learned may be useful in a large number of countries with slow vaccine roll-out due to vaccine hesitancy, particularly among HCWs where there is no vaccine mandate, or unequal access to vaccine supplies.
source: Nevertheless, the lessons learned may be useful in a large number of countries with slow vaccine roll-out due to vaccine hesitancy, particularly among HCWs where there is no vaccine mandate, or unequal access to vaccine supplies (The Lancet Infectious Diseases, 2021).
evidence: Inference about applicability with citation

claim: Nosocomial outbreaks of SARS-CoV-2 still occur despite high vaccination coverage.
source: Furthermore, nosocomial outbreaks of SARS-CoV-2 still occur despite high vaccination coverage (Burugorri-Pierre et al., 2021; Shitrit et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Burugorri-Pierre et al., 2021 and Shitrit et al., 2021

claim: Strategies to prevent nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission in geriatric settings should take into account the potential for patient-to-patient transmission.
source: In conclusion, strategies to prevent nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission in geriatric settings should take into account the potential for patient-to-patient transmission and the transmission dynamics between HCWs in non-Covid wards, which our study suggests may differ from those in dedicated Covid-19 wards.
evidence: Inference drawn from study findings

claim: Strategies to prevent nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission in geriatric settings should take into account the transmission dynamics between HCWs in non-Covid wards, which may differ from those in dedicated Covid-19 wards.
source: In conclusion, strategies to prevent nosocomial SARS-CoV-2 transmission in geriatric settings should take into account the potential for patient-to-patient transmission and the transmission dynamics between HCWs in non-Covid wards, which our study suggests may differ from those in dedicated Covid-19 wards.
evidence: Inference drawn from study findings

claim: Most importation events were linked to HCW.
source: Most importation events were linked to HCW.

claim: Transmission between HCWcovid was more limited than transmission between patients and HCWoutbreak.
source: Unexpectedly, transmission between HCWcovid was more limited than transmission between patients and HCWoutbreak.
evidence: Direct statement in abstract summarizing findings

claim: This finding highlights gaps in infection control and suggests the possible areas of improvements to limit the extent of nosocomial transmission.
source: This finding highlights gaps in infection control and suggests the possible areas of improvements to limit the extent of nosocomial transmission.

source: We estimated that 16 importation events occurred with high confidence (4 patients, 12 HCWs) that jointly led to up to 41 secondary cases; in six additional cases (5 HCWs, 1 patient), importation was possible with a posterior probability between 10% and 50%.

claim: In six additional cases (5 HCWs, 1 patient), importation was possible with a posterior probability between 10% and 50%.
source: We estimated that 16 importation events occurred with high confidence (4 patients, 12 HCWs) that jointly led to up to 41 secondary cases; in six additional cases (5 HCWs, 1 patient), importation was possible with a posterior probability between 10% and 50%.

claim: The modelling analysis modified the ward attribution for three patients.
source: The modelling analysis modified the ward attribution for three patients.
